articles.title: 科学家们在何处为人工智能体划定界限
articles.originalTitle: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
articles.summary: 这条新闻与智能体相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：Hugging Face：智能体相关动态
articles.fullContent: 将研究任务委派给人工智能并不能免除科学家对工作完成方式的责任。 例如，使用人工智能来查阅文献的研究人员需要核查系统是否忽视了相互矛盾的证据，或者是否提出了被引用的论文不支持的论断。 将数据分析交给智能体系统的人需要了解该系统使用了哪些方法、访问了哪些文件，以及结果是否能够成功重现。 将实验室规程的某一部分自动化的研究人员需要确信系统遵守物理安全限制，例如温度限制或材料毒性；而处理人类参与者数据的研究人员则需要确信系统能够保护参与者的隐私，并限制谁可以访问他们的信息。 研究人员还需要有明确的机构指南，用于核验和披露人工智能辅助的工作。 这些伦理和安全问题是我们“AI助力科学”工作的核心。 负责任的科学不仅仅关乎准确性——由于科学家和科学界过去的行动和选择，科学领域存在着伦理研究规范，这些规范还涵盖了研究的开展方式及其影响。 我们希望人工智能工具能够拓展科学家所能完成的工作，同时又不影响他们仔细审查证据、验证方法以及——也许最重要的是——为自己的研究结果负责的能力。 为了更好地了解这需要什么，我们采访了17位从事自然科学、应用科学和社会科学工作的科学家，就负责任地开发人工智能代理进行了访谈。 这些系统可以使用工具，并以不同程度的自主性执行研究任务。 这些访谈借鉴了通过早期调查工作建立的研究人员网络——我们希望了解科学家将如何引导人工智能的发展，以反映其所在领域的责任。 我们询问了研究人员在哪些方面会欢迎智能体协助、可能出现哪些问题，以及他们需要哪些保障措施才能放心地让智能体参与自己的研究。 我们对这些问题的兴趣源于评估Ai2开发的模型安全性的工作。 随着我们越来越多地关注用于科学的人工智能，我们发现，科学应用方面的许多安全工作都强调生物学和核物理学等领域的灾难性风险。 我们还需要有方法来评估智能体是否在其应用领域遵守负责任研究行为的标准。 我们的主要发现之一与信任有关。 在所有访谈中，我们确定了科学信任的五个维度：验证、隐私、客观性、问责制和透明度。 这些维度共同反映了人们的关切，而这些关切超出了人工智能系统是否给出正确答案的范畴。 研究人员还需要了解答案是如何得出的，保护敏感信息，识别偏见，并确定由谁负责核查人工智能辅助得出的结果并为其背书。 这些都是负责任地开展研究的问题。 另一项主要发现表明，科学家应协助决定代理应承担哪些研究任务、这些代理如何运作以及如何评估其表现。 即使结果在技术上是正确的，如果研究人员无法检查其生成方式，或者如果代理访问了超出研究人员授权范围的机密数据或文件，那么该结果可能也不适合用于科学研究。

articles.fullContent: 亚马逊对Meta的AI代理Muse的态度可能有所转变。 据报道，这两家科技巨头正在商讨一项潜在的交易，该交易将使Meta广受欢迎的AI代理能够直接连接到亚马逊的商店。 此次谈判将标志着与短短两个月前的重大转变，当时Muse用户发现他们无法在亚马逊上购买产品，而是在尝试结账时收到了错误消息。 据《财富》周三的报道，援引知情人士透露，亚马逊和Meta就此事进行了多轮谈判。 仍有两大关键问题有待商定：在潜在协议下，如何展示搜索结果，以及如何处理广告。 亚马逊最关心的事项之一是，像 Muse 这样的第三方购物代理商会如何影响其广告业务。 10 月，亚马逊首席执行官安迪·贾西（Andy Jassy）表示，很少有顾客通过外部购物代理进行购买。 亚马逊也可能一直在等待 Muse 成熟，然后再同意将其与自己的平台整合。 如果 Muse 下错订单或在购物过程中造成问题，最终可能由亚马逊来处理不满的顾客和不开心的卖家。 《财富》杂志报道称，据知情人士透露，高管们担心第三方购物代理可能会削弱亚马逊与消费者的直接关系。 据《财富》杂志报道，亚马逊与Meta之间任何潜在的协议都需要得到两家公司首席执行官的批准。 Meta 和亚马逊尚未回应 TechCrunch 的置评请求。 每周工作日和周日，您都可以获得TechCrunch的精彩报道。 TechCrunch Mobility是您获取交通运输新闻和见解的理想之地。 初创企业是TechCrunch的核心，因此请每周接收我们最精彩的报道。 为有影响力的人物提供他们开始新的一天所需的信息。

articles.title: GPT-6模型展现出内在的蛋白质设计能力
articles.originalTitle: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
articles.summary: 这条新闻与大模型、推理相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：OpenAI：大模型、推理相关动态
articles.fullContent: 我们的GPT‑6系列模型仅使用推理和代码即可设计出新的蛋白质形状及其化学结构单元的序列，而无需调用专门的生物学模型来生成这些设计。 在许多蛋白质设计任务中，一个内部研究模型与专业模型表现相当或更胜一筹。 研究人员还可以通过提示模型蛋白质应附着的位置及其应采取的形状来指导设计。 在与Onava的实验室测试中，基于GPT‑6.2设计的蛋白质显示出在五个靶标上具有结合或附着作用的证据。 经过重新设计的抗体也保留了结合能力。 专用模型有助于提供序列并选择候选物进行测试。 这些模型的书面推理和代码表明，它们借鉴了数学、物理学、化学和生物学知识，来推理蛋白质的形状及其与其他分子的相互作用。 在一篇题为《GPT‑6 作为蛋白质生物学的通用基础模型：超越专用模型》的预印本中，我们展示了我们的 GPT‑6 系列模型具有设计新蛋白质的固有能力：这些模型仅使用推理和通用编码工具，无需依赖专用生物学模型，即可设计出新的蛋白质结构和序列。 蛋白质在活细胞中承担着大量工作。 它们驱动维持生命的化学反应，通过血液输送氧气，并保护身体免受感染。 形状不正确的蛋白质也可能导致疾病和功能障碍。 蛋白质由称为氨基酸的化学结构单元链构成。 这些氨基酸的排列顺序（或称序列）有助于决定蛋白质如何折叠成三维形状，而这又会影响蛋白质的功能。 科学家们通常一开始就对他们希望蛋白质发挥的作用有明确的认识。 他们可能希望蛋白质能够阻断帮助癌细胞逃避免疫系统的信号，或者帮助从空气中捕获二氧化碳。 挑战在于弄清楚哪种三维结构能使蛋白质发挥作用，以及哪种氨基酸序列能赋予它这种结构。 能够生成三维蛋白质结构和序列的专业生物学模型使这项工作更具实用性。 使用和协调这些专用模型需要具备丰富的专业知识。 每个模型都接受特定类型的输入和约束，如果不更改其软件或进行额外训练，这些模型就无法轻松接受新类型的信息。 相比之下，能够执行多个专用模型工作的通用模型可以轻松适应新的指令和要求。 我们的研究展示了将自然语言与蛋白质的固有能力相结合的潜在威力。 我们可以指导我们的模型，其规模范围从两个原子之间的单键到蛋白质的整体形状。 例如，我们询问了GPT-6。 2 来预测小分子会在哪里以及如何与蛋白质结合。 当我们已经知道哪两个原子形成了键时，就可以将该信息提供给模型，并询问分子的其余部分将如何匹配。 我们只需更改提示，即可在这些任务之间切换，而无需重新训练模型。

articles.fullContent: ChatGPT 和 Codex 集成可帮助 Clay 用户研究交易，并将数据转化为市场进入策略，而 GPT-6 模型则负责推理。 即使销售团队拥有大量关于潜在客户的数据，他们仍然可能难以弄清哪些因素最重要，并制定出成功的推销方案。 Clay ⁠（在新窗口中打开）是一款旨在提供帮助的自学习营收引擎。 借助GPT‑6 Astra、GPT‑6 Sol和其他模型，Clay让用户能够创建公司和人员列表，使用代理丰富这些记录，并将这些信息用于市场进入策略。 Clay 还将这些功能带到客户已经在使用的 Codex 和 ChatGPT 插件中，让创建和运行入市工作流程以及研究客户和交易变得更加容易。 “ChatGPT 中的 Clay 为销售代表提供了一种方式，让他们能够更深入地了解他们试图推销的客户。 它将所有这些丰富的背景信息带到他们已经在使用的工具中。” Clay 的 Codex 集成让构建者能够在 Codex 中创建和运行入市策略，同时让销售代表能够访问数据，用于研究客户或了解他们正在努力达成的交易。 Jeff 曾看到销售代表将自己系统中的信息与公共数据集相结合，以确定如何最有效地向客户传达其产品的价值。 “客户喜欢使用 Codex 完成销售中的许多不同任务，”他说。 “我们看到，最优秀的销售代表从中受益最大。” Clay 的 ChatGPT 插件将相同的客户数据引入销售代表已在使用的另一款工具，帮助他们在不离开 ChatGPT 的情况下进一步了解潜在客户。 Jeff 表示：“这取得了巨大成功。” OpenAI 模型为 Claygent 的研究、资格认定、数据扩充和信号检测提供支持，并为帮助用户构建工作流程和协调其他 Clay 代理的代理提供支持。 Clay 将 GPT‑6 Sol 作为其主要模型，使用 GPT‑6 Astra 处理更难的任务，使用 GPT‑6 Luna 处理对成本敏感的工作。 该系列支持背景研究和文案撰写，以及用户直接与之合作的代理。 通过Responses API，Clay可以经由同一个接口使用不同级别的智能和成本。 “在不同的价格点使用相同的Responses API，这是OpenAI模型对我们来说非常有吸引力的一点。”Jeff表示。 GPT‑6 Astra 还能帮助 Jeff 构建和测试软件。 他过去曾花大量时间手动检查自己构建的功能；现在，他可以让 GPT‑6 Astra 处理更多此类工作。 他解释道：“GPT‑6 Astra真正改变了我构建软件的方式，因为它完全闭合了工程流程的闭环。 现在，我可以让Astra编写代码、添加测试，然后实际运行测试并测试功能，再将结果记录下来并上传到PR中。 这大大简化了我的工作。 ”

articles.fullContent: Remote Agents Platform将工程任务转化为API调用：团队委派工作，执行在远程沙盒中进行，结果以合并请求的形式返回。 在内部安全平台上，修复的漏洞数量增加了一倍多。iFood维护着15,000多个代码仓库。 每个项目都需要定期执行特定任务：验证代码以确保其符合内部标准、修复存在漏洞的依赖项或运行分析。 这些任务本身都不难。 挑战在于这些任务成倍增加时。 “为一个代码仓库解决这个问题很容易。 挑战在于大规模解决问题。”iFood高级软件工程师Victor Coelho表示。 “远程代理平台旨在使我们能够大规模地在所有 15,000 个代码仓库中解决这个问题。” 在平台上线之前，每个团队都以自己的方式来解决问题，但他们都遇到了同样的障碍。 “以前，我们的解决方案是零散的。 想象一下，iFood 的几个团队试图解决不同的问题，但他们没有这一层，没有这个可供他们使用的代理运行时。 最终，这些解决方案总是会遇到同样的问题。 “我们缺少的不是智能或用例。 而是执行基础设施。 一个专用的运行时。该团队将远程代理平台描述为一个启动远程代理式编码任务的 API。 该周期有三个步骤：用户通过 REST 调用提交提示和环境要求；平台在隔离沙盒内的专用远程 Runner 上处理任务；稍后检索结果。 “平台的入口点，即其接口，是一个简单的REST API。 用户可以使用此API创建他们需要的运行。 在内部，我们处理和管理整个生命周期，并将执行委托给隔离的沙盒。”他解释道。 可以实时监控任务进度。 Runner的内部设计在两种不同类型的步骤之间交替进行，这种组合使整个工作流程具有可预测性。 确定性步骤贯穿工作流程的始末：在开始时克隆代码仓库、导入代理可使用的技能并设置工作分支；在结束时发布合并请求并使生成的工件可用。 介于两者之间的是运行 GPT‑5 的代理执行本身。6 沙盒中的 Luna。 “这是这两者的结合：工作流中的确定性步骤和代理执行。”

articles.fullContent: Richpanel 使用 GPT‑6 Astra 和 GPT‑6。1 Sol 为其 AI 客服专员提供工具和流程，并使用 GPT‑6 Luna 进行对话。 除了知道如何回应客户的请求外，AI 支持专员还需要能够执行解决方案。 为此，他们需要能够使用合适的工具和说明。 据 Richpanel 首席执行官 Amit RG 介绍，人工客服代表在为客户提供服务时可能会使用 20 或 30 种工具，而他们遵循的流程可能从未被记录下来。 Richpanel ⁠（在新窗口中打开）使用OpenAI模型解决了这个问题，既可以设置AI客服专员采取行动和处理客户对话所需的工具，也可以设置所需的程序。 “智能不再是瓶颈。 而是围绕它的所有东西。 “部署支持代理通常需要一名前线部署工程师将代理连接到客户的系统，并确定其工作方式。 Amit发现许多公司没有多余的工程师，于是他问自己：“如果前线部署的工程师本身就是一名AI代理呢？” 于是，Richpanel 打造了这个产品：一个负责处理代理设置的 AI 管理员。 客户开始称之为 Boss AI。 它编写程序，并定义 Richpanel 的一线支持专员、Copilot 和质量保证专员如何调用他们所需的工具。 Richpanel 使用 GPT‑6 Astra 和 GPT‑6. 1 Sol for Boss AI，在构建其他客服代表将遵循的工具和程序时，优先考虑准确性。 Richpanel 设计的一线客服代表能够处理数十万次对话，因此每次互动的成本成为模型选择的一个重要考量因素。 它使用 GPT‑6 Luna 和其他 OpenAI 模型来完成这项工作。 Amit 表示，Richpanel 对其 Copilot 和质量保证客服代表也采取了同样的方法。 “关键在于成本和智能之间的平衡。”Amit 表示。 Richpanel 的客户可能已经在使用低成本的外包支持服务。 与这一起点相比，实现运营自动化必须具有财务意义。 Amit认为，OpenAI提供了能够处理长上下文和更长任务的模型，同时保持了成本效益。 Richpanel 可以使用更深入的推理来培训其客服专员，并使用更经济的模型来开展后续的对话。 在2026年10月的采访中，Amit表示，Richpanel在过去六个月内完成了约300次AI客户支持部署。

articles.fullContent: 一款开源运行时，可帮助运维人员保护正在运行的 Linux 系统，无需等待补丁或重启OpenAI 和思科正在推出 Shirudo，这是一款开源运行时，可帮助团队在推出补丁的同时保护 Linux 系统。 在一次受控测试中（在新窗口中打开） ，由 Codex 生成的防护机制阻止了针对正在运行的 Elasticsearch 服务的 Java4Shell 漏洞利用尝试，且无需重启。 我们诚邀整个行业的开发者、安全研究人员和基础设施运营商共同参与，帮助进一步推进该项目的发展。 该项目汇集了OpenAI的前沿人工智能、安全和基础设施研究以及思科的基础设施和安全专长，以帮助保护人们每天依赖的系统。 测试和部署补丁仍可能需要数天或数周的时间。 与此同时，保护服务可能具有挑战性，因为漏洞利用和合法请求可能依赖于相同的Linux操作。 完全阻止该操作可能会使服务离线。 Shirudo（日语意为“盾牌”）旨在帮助安全团队应对这种权衡。 团队可以测试一种名为“盾”的临时防护措施是否能够阻止暴露漏洞的行为，同时允许合法请求通过。 一旦操作员批准了防护，就可以在服务继续运行的同时进行部署。 Shirudo 使用 eBPF，这是一种 Linux 技术，允许小型程序在操作系统内的特定点运行。 这使得观察可疑活动并对正在运行的系统应用有针对性的安全保护成为可能。 Guardian 代理如何使用 eBPF 观察和保护正在运行的系统。 OpenAI 和思科正在围绕四项核心功能设计 Shirudo：实时保护：eBPF 屏蔽功能可以在不重启系统的情况下阻止易受攻击的代码路径。 安全团队可以在实施拟议的防护之前，先监测该防护会对应用程序产生怎样的影响。 以机器速度进行防御：OpenAI 和思科正在设计 Shirudo，旨在为代理提供可编程控制功能，以便调查漏洞、开发有针对性的防护措施，并验证其针对漏洞利用和实际工作负载的有效性。 安全团队控制部署的内容。 可信部署：Shield 在加载前经过加密签名和验证。 Linux 的 eBPF 验证器根据其安全规则检查 eBPF 程序，而内核安全控制则限制未经授权的更改。 硬件支持的验证：Shirudo 使用可信平台模块 (TPM) 来支持加载或移除保护的可验证记录。 运营商可以使用这些证据来检查系统是否符合其安全要求。
articles.originalSummary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences . But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines . If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place. Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement. But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process. Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

articles.fullContent: 从远处看，现代人工智能的构建方式似乎与过去几十年中软件的构建方式相似：使用一套多样化的技术来针对特定的功能。 确实有各种各样的方法，但它们大多不是从零开始设计，而是利用来自一个更简单、更难解释的过程的智能：在一个非常庞大的数据语料库上训练一个压缩器（或等效地（在新窗口中打开） ，预测器）。 1 我认为，跟踪训练更好压缩器的进展速度是理解人工智能发展轨迹的关键。 在本文中，我主张将困惑度（或等效的交叉熵损失）确立为一种指标，用于在模型开发者之间进行比较，并为共同的安全标准提供参考。 作为第一步，我将让OpenAI的预训练进展更加透明。 我们对发布内部困惑度测量结果进行了慎重考虑；这样做会让竞争对手更清楚地了解我们的立场，但与在整个行业建立共同的（在新窗口中打开）安全措施的紧迫性相比，这种顾虑显得微不足道。 我们OpenAI希望此举能成为迈向为未来的步伐控制工作建立共同科学基础的一步。 对人工智能发展的看法，一种简单但本质上具有启发性的观点是：首先，人们构建一台大型计算机，然后使用它在一个大型非结构化数据集上对一个模型（压缩器）进行预训练，接着在不同的语境中应用各种技术——如提示、微调或强化学习——以激发该模型的潜在能力。 算法的进步可能会模糊训练阶段之间的界限，但我们仍然可以将人工智能的创造（我之前称之为“外星人的思维”）与随后有针对性的诱导区分开来，因为人工智能具有难以预测的涌现能力。 多年来，我们衡量这一关键“智能基质”进展的主要方式一直保持着显著的稳定性——我们一直在跟踪模型在留出数据集上的困惑度。 2 , 3困惑度衡量的是模型平均预测下一个token的准确性；困惑度越低，预测越准确。 本文开头展示的图表显示了从 GPT-3 开始，这一指标在我们模型中的演变情况。5. 主要通过这一指标来描述的模型能力范围令人惊叹。 GPT-2 在旧数据集上树立了新的困惑度最高水平 4 ，可以说是有史以来第一个能够持续生成连贯文本段落的模型。 下一个重大飞跃是 GPT-3，它能够在给定任务的几个示例的情况下进行上下文学习。 GPT-3.5 在我们当前的主要评估数据集上的对数困惑度约为 0.99，能够进行流利的对话，并构成了最初的 ChatGPT 的基础。GPT-4 的对数困惑度约为 0.

articles.fullContent: Hebbia 在 GPT‑6 Astra 的测试中看到了金融研究方面的收益。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，领先于表现最佳的替代方案的百分点数。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，与问题相关的引用摘录的百分比。 Hebbia 测试中满足适用呈现要求的百分比。 在演示文稿要求方面，领先于所测试的最佳替代方案的百分点数。 在向客户推荐收购之前，银行家需要弄清财务报表、客户合同和管理层演示文稿。 Hebbia 的 Matrix 有助于整合这些研究，将答案与背后的文件联系起来。 Hebbia 测试了 OpenAI 的 GPT‑6 Astra，以改进这项工作的两个方面：找到问题所需的来源，并根据银行家的简要说明制作演示文稿。 具体运作方式可能是这样的：一位银行家正在帮助客户评估对一家工业软件公司的战略收购，需要审核大约 2000 个文件。 是什么让其收入具有可持续性？ 它与同行相比如何？ 在Hebbia的假设示例中，银行家可以将数据室加载到Matrix中，并在引用的单元格中查看客户集中度、合同条款和流失率。 Matrix可以引入同行备案和行业新闻，帮助制定交易论证，然后将该研究转化为公司的模板中的尽职调查摘要和估值演示文稿。 在该工作流程中，GPT‑6 Astra 会选择文件或 Matrix 单元格来支持答案，然后将分析转换为遵循用户结构和指南的原生 PowerPoint 幻灯片。 “可追溯性对我们的用户来说非常重要，因为他们要根据 AI 实际给出的结果来做出价值数百万美元的决策，”Kavita 表示。 “引用有助于实现可追溯性，并让用户确信人工智能找到了正确的答案。” 在 Hebbia 的测试中，GPT‑6 Astra 将更广泛的来源覆盖范围与高度相关的引用相结合。它获得了 13 分。 在引用所需类型的来源方面，比测试的最佳替代方案高出6个百分点，而其引用的摘录中有99.5%与问题相关。 Hebbia 于 2026 年 8 月至 9 月测试了一个预发布版本，对每个模型使用了相同的金融研究案例和评分标准。 领域专家根据源文档撰写或审核了标准。

articles.fullContent: 我们如何应对蒸馏的安全风险，以及我们在加强整个行业的安全保障方面所吸取的经验教训。 随着前沿人工智能模型的能力不断增强，保障措施在如何负责任地使用这些模型方面发挥着越来越重要的作用。 对抗性蒸馏为不法分子在没有适当保障措施的情况下复制这些能力开辟了一条途径。 行为者可能会在未经授权的情况下使用前沿模型的输出，来训练另一个具有类似功能的模型，然后将其部署，而没有提供同等水平的保护。 例如，攻击者可能会提炼出一个模型的网络能力，并使用由此产生的模型来帮助实施网络攻击，而原始模型本会拒绝协助此类攻击，或者其安全防护措施本会阻止此类攻击。 我们将分享OpenAI如何检测和阻止对抗性蒸馏，我们如何加强对模型受保护推理的保护，以及我们学到了哪些可以帮助加强整个行业的防御措施的经验。 我们处理对抗性蒸馏的方法将对抗性测试、模型训练、分类器和API级保护与对有组织地提取模型能力的企图的调查相结合。 这些更新后的保障措施与我们在生物学和网络安全领域所采用的措施更加一致。 我们特别重视防止攻击者提取我们模型的受保护推理：即模型在努力得出答案的过程中在内部生成的中间步骤，称为其“思维链”。 这些痕迹可能包含最终答案中未提及的信息，因此它们对于另一个模型来说是特别有价值的训练数据。 我们在 GPT‑6 中加强了针对受保护推理提取的防御。2 Astra 和 GPT‑6。2 Sol。在一次使用强大自动化红队的内部自适应评估中，我们测试了攻击者是否能够恢复模型在回答先前提示时生成的受保护推理。 平均攻击成功率从针对具有原始安全防护措施的 GPT‑6 Astra 的 54. 0% 下降到针对具有更新版安全防护措施的 GPT‑6. 2 Astra（采用更新后的安全措施）的攻击成功率降至 0.2%。 蒸馏是一种常见的机器学习技术，其中一个模型从另一个模型产生的数据中学习。 例如，一个模型可以从另一个模型的答案、其推理或其对哪些答案更好以及为什么更好的判断中学习。 除了知识产权问题外，未经授权的蒸馏还会带来严重的安全风险。 通过对抗性蒸馏，第二个模型可以学习先进的前沿能力，而无需继承规范原始模型如何使用这些能力的保障措施。 在网络安全和生物学等双用途领域，这种担忧尤为明显。 一个帮助防御者发现软件漏洞的模型也可能帮助攻击者利用这些漏洞；一个协助生物学研究的模型也可能帮助某人开发有害病原体。 如果将此类能力转移到具有较弱保障措施的模型，该模型可能会提供原始模型会拒绝或原始保障措施会阻止的帮助。 我们的模型可帮助用户完成编码和防御性网络安全任务。 在许多此类良性输出上进行训练的第二个模型可能会学到同样适用于进攻性网络安全任务的技能。

articles.rawFullText: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming. It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

articles.rawFullText: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .  You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

articles.rawFullText: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. articles.fullContent: 多年来，企业一直将人工智能视为一系列独立的实验。 如今，随着人工智能代理开始进入支撑业务运营的工作流程，这种模式开始显得力不从心。 从孤立的试点转向 AI 代理和自主工作流程的组织正面临着一个更深层次的挑战：重新思考数据、业务流程、治理和人员如何相互配合，将 AI 从一系列工具转变为企业运营模式的一部分。 对于SAP业务人工智能平台生态系统高级副总裁兼全球负责人Thorsten Leiduck来说，这种转变始于将人工智能视为一个企业平台，而不是一系列互不关联的项目。 “人工智能完全依赖于数据基础，”他表示，并认为企业需要一个互联且语义丰富的层来反映其业务，然后才能在各个流程中可靠地部署人工智能。 随着人工智能进入任务关键型工作流程，其利害关系也会发生变化。 他说，对于一些日常应用来说，“80%可能就足够好了”，但在供应链或财务结算等领域，这样的准确率“是一个非常糟糕的结果”。这一基础还决定了哪些人工智能应用值得追求。 Infosys SAP BAIP和SAP AI战略北美区副总裁Satinder Pal Singh将AI代理称为“数字同事”，并建议从三个角度评估潜在用例：影响、可行性和可扩展性。 公司应确定代理可以在哪些方面推动有意义的业务指标，确定其数据和人才是否能够支持该用例，然后确定成功的应用是否可以复制。 “无法扩展的试点项目只是一项实验，”他说。 扩展还会使治理问题更加突出。 明确的政策、访问控制、监控和监督是必要的，以确保代理始终值得信赖并符合业务要求。 “缺乏治理并不会加快人工智能的采用，”Singh 表示。 “它会造成风险积压”，最终可能迫使企业进行更具破坏性的停用和审计。 随着人工智能代理作为数字同事承担更多责任，这些考虑因素将变得更加重要。 两位高管都展望着一个未来，即代理系统协调跨应用程序的工作，而针对具体客户的知识图谱和受管控的数据将成为关键的企业资产。 在Singh看来，长期的机会在于将人工智能从生产力工具转变为“决策合作伙伴”，帮助领导者了解当前情况、预测未来发展并确定应对方式。 本期《商业实验室》由Infosys合作制作。

articles.rawFullText: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion. Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation. This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that’s a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap. What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn’t recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start. And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you’re not building AI today, you’re not standing still, you’re falling behind at an accelerating rate. Megan: Right. There’s a real polarization there, isn’t there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity? Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it’s a technology rollout. Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale. Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation. In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that’s what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios. And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps. And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well. Megan: Right. It’s been really clear, isn’t it, on what you’re looking to achieve and what’s worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten’s framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously. The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction. Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what’s the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three. Megan: That’s such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example. Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that’s why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it’s very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side. One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that’s why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company’s reality and not just in generic patterns. And then, I think, the second element that’s important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result. The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that’s why it’s important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system. And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable. Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier? Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership. SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP’s industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement. In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months. What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations . That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel. Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms? Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars. The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed. Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together. Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC. With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that’s part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform. And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework. And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they’re integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire. Megan: Fantastic. That’s a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they’ve used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I’ll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP’s three pillar look like in production. The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys’ agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million. The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That’s the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept. Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what’s your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP? Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you’re absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it’s important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they’re public models. Depending on the provider’s policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk. So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they’re lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That’s why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit. And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical. As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP. Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack? Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That’s the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront. What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical. The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower. The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren’t just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what’s running, what it’s consuming, and whether it’s performing as expected. That’s what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset. And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle. Megan: That’s such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we’ve covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we’ve spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer? Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak. Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs. On the technology front, I think there’s still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we’ll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there’s an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable. And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future. Megan: Which is, of course, what we’re aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten’s architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take. The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That’s not a dashboard. That’s a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains. What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP’s prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for. The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available. So, the next frontier isn’t that AI can do more work. It’s that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that’s where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence. Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today. That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. articles.fullContent: 这篇文章最初刊登在我们的每周人工智能通讯《The Algorithm》上。 如需第一时间在您的收件箱中收到此类报道，请在此处订阅。 周五，一份要求恢复黄仁勋担任英伟达首席执行官的请愿书开始在社交媒体上流传，到周一，请愿书上列出了一些知名签名人，包括埃隆·马斯克和几位有影响力的英伟达研究人员。 但仔细梳理一下这11.5万多个名字，您就会发现，黄仁勋的支持者中有一个庞大的派系——来自AI模型共享平台Hugging Face的高层，以及风险投资公司Andreessen Horowitz和红杉资本——他们都来自科技界的某个特定群体。 这些名字在开源人工智能的发展中有着既得利益，与ChatGPT或Claude不同，这些模型可以下载并独立于大型科技公司运行。 这种模式的支持者表示，如果将人工智能集中在少数几家实力雄厚的公司手中，其他人就会陷入更加不利的境地（如果不是有这么多开源倡导者同时也是风险投资家，他们会在初创公司能够利用更便宜的人工智能而无需向大型科技公司付费时从中获利，那么这种担忧在左翼人工智能行业批评者中听起来就不会显得格格不入）。 黄仁勋已成为向政策制定者捍卫开源事业的领军人物，以应对人们的担忧，即此类模型没有安全防护措施，并将人工智能的领导地位拱手让给中国，而最强大、最受欢迎的开源模型正是诞生于中国。 他们现在希望这位最有影响力的代言人重返岗位。 但威胁到他（以及英伟达）作为开源人工智能倡导者的信誉的，不仅仅是黄仁勋的婚外情。 一项针对中国使用英伟达芯片的初创企业的新研究，以及美国商务部周一宣布的一项新规定，可能会对该运动的声誉及其技术进步造成打击。 周四，也就是黄辞职的那天，前OpenAI研究员Will DePue在网上发布了研究结果，表明中国的人工智能公司获得英伟达先进的Blackwell芯片的渠道比此前估计的要多得多。 中国被禁止使用英伟达最尖端的芯片，以帮助保护美国在人工智能领域的领先地位。 目前尚不清楚他们是如何获得这些芯片的。 DePue声称，这些结果已得到OpenAI和Anthropic高级研究人员的验证，但独立分析尚未证实这些结果。 （DePue未回复采访请求。 英伟达未立即回应置评请求。 )调查结果并未证实英伟达帮助中国公司获得芯片，而且众所周知，芯片走私这一更广泛的问题早已超出英伟达的控制范围。 但这些调查结果暗示，英伟达可能从中国人工智能初创企业的崛起中获益，而美国公司越来越多地使用这些初创企业的模型，而不是国内的替代产品，这确实让黄仁勋陷入了尴尬的境地。 他一直倡导将开源人工智能作为加强美国技术领先地位的一种方式。 去年12月，他在一次关于帮助美国在与中国的AI竞赛中取胜的演讲中表示：“如果没有开源，初创企业就无法蓬勃发展，大学研究人员就无法开展研究，你就无法教授AI，科学家就无法使用AI。” 这也让黄仁勋复职的希望更加渺茫。

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

articles.rawFullText: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”
